title: Lalita's hymn of names
hook: a hymn that opens with names, and never stops naming
carry: in a sahasranama, saying the name is the prayer
tomorrow: what if the Sita who was carried off wasn't really Sita?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Lalita rose from the gods' fire with a sugarcane bow, and your line: desire isn't the enemy; it belongs inside dharma. A hymn with no story, only names: why would that work?

Look at how different people have you saved in their phones. A parent has one name for you. A best friend, another. A grandmother might have five, depending on her mood. Here's an old hymn that does that on purpose. It opens: Shri Mata. Shri Maharajni. Shrimat Simhasaneshvari. Then another name, and another, on and on. No story told in sentences, no request at the end. Just names. It's the Lalita Sahasranama, and tradition places it in the Brahmanda Purana, right after yesterday's story. So, the puzzle: why would a hymn be made of nothing but names?
screen: `HOW ARE YOU SAVED IN THEIR PHONES?` → `SHRI MATA. SHRI MAHARAJNI.` → `WHY ONLY NAMES?`

segments.voice: First clue: listen to what the names say. Shri Mata: the holy mother. Shri Maharajni: the great queen. Shrimat Simhasaneshvari: the queen on the lion throne. Then two names that are yesterday's story, folded small. Chidagni kunda sambhuta: born from the fire pit of consciousness. Deva karya samudyata: risen to do the work of the gods. So the names carry the story. Someone who knows the Lalitopakhyana hears the whole battle inside a few words. The frame is the same, too: Hayagriva teaches Agastya, and tradition says the names were first sung by goddesses of speech, at Lalita's own command. Second clue: a name is said to someone. A description talks about a person; a name turns toward her. Each one faces one more side of the same goddess: mother, queen, the girl who rose from the fire. Third clue: said one after another, the names add up to a portrait no single sentence could hold. That's the answer, and it's one of the oldest Hindu practices: saying the names of God. There are hymns of names for Vishnu and for Shiva too, and many families say one at home. For the people who say them, the names aren't praise with the content left out. Saying the name is the prayer. Some devotees recite the whole hymn; some keep a few names close and come back to them.
screen: `THE NAMES CARRY THE STORY.` · `A NAME IS SAID TO SOMEONE.` · `MOTHER, QUEEN, GIRL FROM THE FIRE.` · then, large: `SAYING THE NAME IS THE PRAYER.`

segments.voice: Say three of today's names out loud, slowly, the way devotees do: Shri Mata. Shri Maharajni. Shrimat Simhasaneshvari. Leave a full breath between each, and let each one turn you toward a different face: mother, queen, the one on the lion throne. If you don't pray, say instead the names the people who love you call you, and notice that none of them cancels the others.
The Brahmanda: the Purana of Brahma's egg, and the home tradition gives Lalita's hymn of names.
Hold onto this one: in a sahasranama, saying the name is the prayer. A goddess praised one name at a time. Back tomorrow.

howItsDone: Many devotees of the goddess recite the Lalita Sahasranama, the hymn of her names, at home or in temples, some daily and some on festival days; others keep a few of its names for quiet repetition. Hymns of names for Vishnu and Shiva are recited the same way.

Lalita Sahasranama.meaning: a hymn made of names for the goddess Lalita

Shri Mata.meaning: the holy mother: the hymn's first name

Shri Maharajni.meaning: the great queen: the hymn's second name

Hayagriva.meaning: the horse-headed form of Vishnu, who teaches the hymn

Agastya.meaning: the sage who hears the hymn
